passage: Playgroup note, rainy July week. Nazia had the block tub today. When Ojas came over, she tipped half the blocks toward him at once: "You gave me your red car yesterday." Then a boy who usually grabs and keeps things reached in. Nazia pulled the tub back. "No. You never give me." He started to cry. I sat with them both and said, "You remember who shares with you. That's fair thinking." Then I gave the boy a turn to share his puzzle with Nazia first. He did. Nazia passed him two blocks. Next: more take-turns games.

qa.q: What did Ojas give Nazia yesterday?
qa.a: His red car.

qa.q: Why did Nazia pull the tub back from the other boy?
qa.a: She felt it was unfair, because he never gives her things; she was annoyed and protective of her blocks.

qa.q: What did the note-writer try next, and why could it help?
qa.a: The boy got a turn to share his puzzle with Nazia first, so she saw him give and was willing to give back.

qa.q: What is it like for the boy when Nazia says "You never give me"?
qa.a: He feels hurt and left out, and cries, perhaps not yet understanding that his grabbing is why she won't share.

grounding: Illustrates a young child sharing with the friend who shared before and refusing one who never does.

passage: Pongal morning, and the village square smelled of sweet rice. Madhuri spun her new paper pinwheel. Tanuja ran up. Yesterday Tanuja had shared her sugarcane. "Here, you blow," Madhuri said, holding it out. Then a bigger cousin came, the one who never let anyone touch his top. "Give!" Madhuri hid the pinwheel behind her. "You didn't give me your top." "So?" "So no." Her grandmother, shelling peanuts nearby, chuckled. "You keep good accounts, little one." The cousin sulked by the well. After a while he rolled his top toward Madhuri's feet. She blinked, then held out the pinwheel.

qa.q: What had Tanuja shared yesterday?
qa.a: Her sugarcane.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when she said "So no"?
qa.a: She felt it was unfair to share with someone who never lets anyone touch his top; she was firm and a little cross.

qa.q: What changed the cousin's luck with the pinwheel?
qa.a: He rolled his top toward Madhuri first, and then she held out the pinwheel; giving first opened the door.

qa.q: How might the cousin feel while sulking by the well?
qa.a: He probably felt left out and annoyed, and perhaps began to see that sharing gets sharing back.

grounding: Shows a young child sharing with the friend who shared before and refusing the one who never shares.

passage: Christmas Eve in Madrid, with thin snow on the park hill. Last week Esther had let Santiago ride her sled three times, so today he waved her over to his red one. "You go first!" Esther whooped all the way down. Then a boy from the building next door marched up. He always kept his scooter to himself. "My turn." Santiago held the rope tight. "You never let me ride your scooter." "That's different." "No, it's the same." His papá said, "Maybe he'll share next time if you share now?" Santiago thought hard, then gave one turn. Just one.

qa.q: How many times had Esther let Santiago ride her sled last week?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Why did Santiago hold the rope tight?
qa.a: He felt it wasn't fair, because the boy always kept his scooter to himself; Santiago was reluctant and a bit indignant.

qa.q: What did Santiago's papá suggest, and why is it a useful idea?
qa.a: That sharing now might lead to sharing next time; it shows the boy a chance to join in the give-and-take.

qa.q: How might Esther feel about being waved over first?
qa.a: She would feel pleased and liked, seeing that her sharing last week was remembered.

grounding: Illustrates a young child sharing with the friend who shared last time and holding back from one who never shares.

passage: The power went out halfway through decorating the building's Navratri stage, and there were only two hours left before garba. By torchlight, Nirmala Aunty handed out the leftover pedas. "Ankita, four for you. You worked hardest." "No!" Ankita's voice rang across the dark courtyard. "That's not fair. The twins carried the chairs. The Joshi boy tied every marigold string. I only held the ladder." "Beta, it's just pedas." "It's not just pedas. Everyone gets three, or I don't want mine." A few adults laughed. Nirmala Aunty sighed and split them again, three each, while the torch flickered. Ankita counted carefully, then nodded, satisfied.

qa.q: How many pedas did Nirmala Aunty first give Ankita?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: Why was Ankita so upset about getting extra?
qa.a: She felt indignant because others had worked as hard or harder; fairness mattered to her more than getting more.

qa.q: What could Ankita try next time she feels something is unfair?
qa.a: She could say it calmly and privately to Aunty, which would still make her point without the whole courtyard hearing.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Aunty see Ankita's outburst?
qa.a: She might feel a little embarrassed and tired in the rush, but also see that Ankita cares deeply about fairness.

grounding: Shows a child keeping track of who helped and objecting loudly to an unequal split even when she would get more.

passage: New Year's Eve in the flat, with fairy lights taped along the window. Papa cut the chocolate cake and slid the biggest slice to Sudha. "For my helper." Sudha pushed it back. "No, Papa. Shankar carried all the chairs up from Mrs Pinto's flat. I only folded napkins." Shankar looked up, surprised. Sudha pulled a small notebook from her pocket. "I wrote it down. Monday, I dried dishes. Tuesday, Shankar watered plants. Today, chairs." Papa laughed. "You keep a register?" "Somebody has to," said Sudha seriously. "Equal slices." Papa cut again, carefully. Shankar grinned and whispered, "Thanks."

qa.q: What did Sudha pull from her pocket?
qa.a: A small notebook.

qa.q: What does Sudha's notebook suggest about how she thinks?
qa.a: It suggests she cares a lot, maybe a bit rigidly, about fairness; she feels uncomfortable taking more than her share and keeps careful track.

qa.q: How could Papa respond to Sudha's register in a helpful way?
qa.a: He could praise her fairness while gently saying that small kindnesses don't always need to be counted.

qa.q: How does Shankar see his sister's protest?
qa.a: He is surprised and grateful, glad she noticed his work with the chairs.

grounding: Illustrates a child keeping score of favours and objecting to an unequal split that favours her.

passage: "Eid Mubarak! Sevaiyan for everyone!" Ammi set the bowls down. "Zainab, the big bowl is yours." "Why mine?" "You helped me roast the vermicelli." "Imran peeled all the almonds. That took forever." Imran looked up from his phone. "It's fine, take it." "It's not fine." Zainab crossed her arms. "Last Eid you got the big bowl because you went to the market. So this time it should be equal, or you should have it." "You remember last Eid?" Ammi asked. "Of course I do." Imran laughed. "She's like a bank." Ammi poured some from the big bowl into Imran's. "Happy now, little judge?" Zainab checked both bowls. "Now it's fair."

qa.q: What did Imran peel?
qa.a: All the almonds.

qa.q: How can you tell Zainab feels strongly about fairness?
qa.a: She crosses her arms, refuses the big bowl, and remembers who got more last Eid; she feels uneasy until the bowls are equal.

qa.q: What would you advise Zainab about keeping score?
qa.a: Caring about fairness is good, but she could let small things go sometimes, since families even out over many Eids.

qa.q: What is it like for Imran when his sister insists on equal bowls?
qa.a: He finds it funny, calling her a bank, but probably also feels noticed for peeling the almonds.

grounding: Shows a child tracking who did what across festivals and objecting to getting the larger share.

passage:
Monday
Arnab asked me today if I could help him with his chemistry project this weekend. I said I had cricket practice. True, but I could have skipped it. The whole walk home I felt sick about it. When I was ill for two weeks in August, Arnab photocopied every single note for me and even wrote a summary. I passed because of him. So why didn't I say yes? Maybe because it feels like I have to. Like there's a bill. And then Arnab said, "No problem, I'll manage," and that made it worse. I'm going to text him. I'll help on Sunday. But I hate that part of me is doing it to feel even again.
Wasim

qa.q: What did Arnab do when Wasim was ill in August?
qa.a: He photocopied every single note and even wrote a summary.

qa.q: What is Wasim feeling on the walk home?
qa.a: Wasim feels guilty and sick about saying no, and a little resentful that the help feels like a bill to be paid.

qa.q: What could Wasim say to Arnab to make the friendship feel less like a ledger?
qa.a: Wasim could say honestly that the August notes meant a lot and that the help now comes from friendship, not from repaying a debt.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel when Wasim says he has cricket practice?
qa.a: Arnab may feel a little let down but hides it with "No problem, I'll manage", not wanting to make Wasim feel obliged.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who received help from a friend feeling the pull to repay it and guilt when it stays unpaid.

qa.q: What is Neelam feeling when writing "i didnt know it came with a price tag"?

qa.a: Reena feels friends should help back, and stress makes the lab record feel like something owed.

passage: All through the winter term, Manjula had let Pallavi use her cycle to ride to the kasba school while Manjula took the bus with her aunt. Pallavi was grateful. She brought Manjula guavas from the tree, braided her hair before exams, and still felt she owed more. One evening at the handpump, Manjula said lightly in front of the other girls, "Pallavi rides my cycle, so she'll carry my water today." The girls laughed. Pallavi carried the pot home, her face hot. She kept thinking: was every guava a payment? That night she told her mother she wanted to walk to school from now on. Her mother said, "Tell Manjula how that felt, instead." Pallavi lay awake, unsure what she wanted.

qa.q: What did Pallavi bring Manjula from the tree?
qa.a: Guavas.

qa.q: Why was Pallavi's face hot as she carried the pot home?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and resentful that Manjula mentioned the cycle in front of the girls, making the kindness feel like a debt.

qa.q: What did Pallavi's mother suggest, and why could it be better than walking?
qa.a: Telling Manjula how it felt; it gives the friendship a chance to be fixed instead of ending the favour silently.

qa.q: How might Manjula have meant her comment?
qa.a: Manjula said it lightly and may have meant it as a joke, not realising it made Pallavi feel owed and exposed.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who received a favour feeling bound to repay it and hurt when it is treated as a debt.

passage: Okay, so you asked why our flat is so quiet in the kitchen now. It's Hansa. When she moved in, we all shared everything. Rice, oil, someone cooks, someone washes. Hansa ate with us every night. Never cooked. Never washed. Once she said, "I'll buy the gas cylinder next time," and then didn't. Nobody said anything. But slowly, people started cooking smaller portions. Bhavna began eating in her room. Last week someone put a note on the fridge: "Please label your food." That note was about Hansa, and everybody knew it. I felt bad, honestly. I don't think anyone has actually talked to her. We just all stopped. I, Sahil, am thinking of being the one who says it straight.

qa.q: What did Hansa say she would buy next time?
qa.a: The gas cylinder.

qa.q: How does Sahil feel about the way the flat has handled Hansa?
qa.a: Sahil feels uncomfortable and a bit guilty, noticing that everyone quietly withdrew and left notes instead of talking to her.

qa.q: What would a wise first step be for Sahil?
qa.a: Talk to Hansa privately and kindly, naming what has been happening and asking whether she can take turns cooking or washing.

qa.q: What is it like for Hansa, if she notices the smaller portions and the fridge note?
qa.a: She might feel shut out and embarrassed without knowing exactly why, since nobody has told her directly.

grounding: Shows a flatmate noticing one person keeps taking without giving and the group withdrawing and leaving pointed notes before any confrontation.

passage: I'm Seema, from Room 14, and I watched the whole thing across our corridor. Sudha always seemed to need something. An iron, a charger, the last packet of biscuits, someone's notes the night before exams. People lent them happily at first. I never once saw her lend anything back; when Latika asked for her umbrella in the rain, Sudha said she was using it, though it was drying on the rail. By the second month, doors that used to stand open were closed when she came down the corridor. At dinner, girls would stop a story when she sat down. Nobody said a word to her face. I can't tell whether Sudha even noticed. She kept smiling and asking. Maybe she didn't know how else to belong.

qa.q: What was Sudha's umbrella doing when she said she was using it?
qa.a: It was drying on the rail.

qa.q: What seems to be going on in Seema's mind as Seema watches Sudha?
qa.a: Seema seems uneasy and a little sympathetic, noticing the group's silent punishment and wondering if Sudha even knows or just wants to belong.

qa.q: What could someone in the corridor do instead of closing doors?
qa.a: One person could talk to Sudha kindly and directly about lending back, giving her a fair chance to change.

qa.q: How might Latika feel about Sudha after the umbrella moment?
qa.a: Latika probably felt irritated and let down, seeing that Sudha takes freely but won't give even when she can.

grounding: Illustrates an observer noticing a free rider and the group punishing her through quiet withdrawal rather than direct confrontation.

passage: Before: On Monday, Nilesh watched Ganga ask to borrow the flat's shared laptop charger again. "Mine's lost." Everyone said sure. She also took the last of the milk and left the empty bottle. During: Two Saturdays later, the flat ordered food together. Ganga said she'd pay next time. That was the third next time. Nilesh noticed the others exchange a look. When Ganga asked who wanted to go to the market, nobody did. The charger quietly disappeared into someone's room. After: A week on, at breakfast, one flatmate said loudly, "Funny how milk vanishes around here." Ganga went red and left. Nilesh stirred his tea, uneasy. It worked, sort of. But nobody had ever just asked her.

qa.q: What did Ganga take on Monday besides the charger?
qa.a: The last of the milk, leaving the empty bottle.

qa.q: What is Nilesh feeling as he stirs his tea?
qa.a: He feels uneasy, seeing that the group's pointed comment embarrassed Ganga and that nobody had ever simply asked her.

qa.q: What could the flatmates have done before the pointed comment?
qa.a: They could have spoken to Ganga calmly early on, naming the charger, milk and food, and agreeing on how to share fairly.

qa.q: How might Ganga see the breakfast comment?
qa.a: Ganga likely felt humiliated and ambushed, going red and leaving, instead of being given a private chance to fix it.

grounding: Shows a flatmate noticing a free rider and the group withdrawing and making a pointed comment before any direct talk.

passage: You want to know why I stopped giving Farida rides? Fair question, since I drive half the office. I'm Deepak, and honestly, I like helping. Last month I drove Sunil to the hospital for his mother, helped Joan move her boxes, covered two shifts for the new guy. Didn't expect anything back. Farida was different. Every day she'd wait by my car. Never once asked if I minded. Once she made me detour to her cousin's place, forty minutes. When my car broke down, she found another lift before I'd finished calling the mechanic. So last Monday I told her, calmly, "I'm not going to do the daily rides anymore." She was annoyed. I still help people. I just watch where it goes.

qa.q: How long was the detour to Farida's cousin's place?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel about telling Farida no?
qa.a: Deepak felt calm and settled about it, having noticed that Farida only took, even though Deepak generally enjoys helping others.

qa.q: What does Deepak's approach show about being generous and setting limits?
qa.a: Deepak keeps helping freely, but when someone habitually takes, Deepak says clearly and calmly that it will stop.

qa.q: How might Farida see Deepak's decision?
qa.a: Farida was annoyed and may feel Deepak suddenly turned cold, not having noticed that she never gave anything back.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who helps generously without counting but calmly stops giving to someone who habitually takes.

passage: I'm Kashish, and I sat next to Jyoti at the accounts office for a year. Everyone went to Jyoti. She fixed people's spreadsheets, stayed back to explain the new software, lent her charger, covered calls. She never kept track that I could see. Then there was Mohan from the next team. He'd send her his reports to "just check", every single week, and take the credit in meetings. One Thursday he dropped another file on her desk. Jyoti looked at it, then at him, and said quietly, "I've helped with these every week. I can't keep doing your reports. I'm happy to show you once how I do the checks." Mohan stared. She went back to her screen. I don't know what she felt inside. Her hands were steady.

qa.q: What did Mohan send Jyoti every single week?
qa.a: His reports to "just check".

qa.q: What might Kashish be feeling while watching Jyoti say no?
qa.a: Kashish seems impressed and a little surprised, noticing how calm and steady Jyoti stayed, while admitting not knowing what she felt inside.

qa.q: Which part of Jyoti's response worked, and why?
qa.a: Offering to show Mohan once how she does the checks worked, because it set a limit but still gave him a fair way to learn.

qa.q: What is it like for Mohan when Jyoti refuses?
qa.a: Mohan is taken aback and may feel embarrassed, suddenly unable to lean on her and take credit.

grounding: Shows an observer describing a young adult who helps generously but calmly refuses a habitual taker.

passage: Day one: Sunaina called Farida at dawn. "Can you drop Pihu at the crèche? My shift started early." Farida went, a little late for her own work. She didn't mind. Day two, the following week: Sunaina asked to borrow Farida's scooter "for an hour" and brought it back at night, tank nearly empty. Farida filled it and said nothing. She'd done the same for her sister, after all. Day three, a month later: Sunaina texted, "Scooter again tmrw? Also can u keep Pihu Sat?" Farida thought of every favour; not one had come back. She called. "Sunaina, I love Pihu. I'll keep her Saturday. But the scooter, no. I need it, and it keeps coming back empty." Her voice was calm. Her heart was pounding.

qa.q: What did Sunaina ask Farida to do on day one?
qa.a: Drop Pihu at the crèche.

qa.q: How was Farida feeling when she called Sunaina on day three?
qa.a: She felt nervous, with her heart pounding, but determined to stay calm and set a fair limit.

qa.q: How did Farida balance generosity and limits?
qa.a: She still offered to keep Pihu on Saturday, a real help, but refused the scooter, naming the reason plainly.

qa.q: How might Sunaina react to Farida's call?
qa.a: Sunaina might feel surprised or a little guilty, realising she had kept taking without giving back.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who helps freely, then calmly declines to keep giving to someone who habitually takes.

passage: Before: In the winter holidays, Harish ran to the colony swing. "You can't play with us," Sahil said. Harish froze, then walked home slowly. "My tummy hurts," he told Mama, and wouldn't eat. During: Two days later, he stayed on the balcony. Mama sat with him. "Did someone leave you out?" He nodded into her shoulder. After: The next Sunday, Mama walked him down and asked Sahil's mother to help the boys take turns. Sahil pushed Harish once on the swing. Harish's tummy felt better by lunch.

qa.q: Where did Harish run to?
qa.a: The colony swing.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when he said his tummy hurt?
qa.a: He felt hurt and sad at being told he couldn't play, and the pain of being left out showed up as a tummy ache.

qa.q: What did Mama do that helped?
qa.a: She asked gently whether someone had left him out, then went with him and asked Sahil's mother to help the boys take turns.

qa.q: What might change for Harish if Mama had only given him tummy medicine?
qa.a: The real hurt of being excluded would be missed, and Harish might keep avoiding the swing.

grounding: Shows a young child told he can't play freezing and saying his tummy hurts, and the hurt easing over days with support.

passage: The wedding hall was packed for the Eid function, and the drums were so loud nobody could hear anything. Sabina found the children's corner. Lalit and three others were building a tower with paper cups. "Can I play?" "No. You can't play with us." Sabina stood very still. Then she ran back through the crowd, but Ammi wasn't at their table. Sabina sat under it, hugging her knees, and cried into her frock. When Ammi finally found her, Sabina whispered, "My tummy hurts." Ammi pulled her onto her lap and held her till the drums stopped.

qa.q: What were Lalit and the others building?
qa.a: A tower with paper cups.

qa.q: What does Sabina's tummy ache suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt deeply hurt and lonely after being shut out, a pain she felt in her body.

qa.q: How could Ammi help Sabina after holding her?
qa.a: She could ask gently what happened, then take her back and help her join the game or find another child to play with.

qa.q: What is it like for Sabina when Ammi isn't at the table?
qa.a: It makes the hurt worse; left out and unable to find her mother in a noisy crowd, she feels alone and scared.

grounding: Illustrates a young child told she cannot play, freezing, crying and saying her tummy hurts.

passage: Holi afternoon in the colony, and the water guns were out. Yash had a gang of four. Deepak ran up with his little yellow pichkari. "Can I play?" "No. You can't play with us. You're too small." Deepak stopped where he was. The pichkari dripped onto his feet. Then he went and sat on the bottom stair, arms around his stomach. "My tummy is hurting," he told his Dadi. Dadi felt his forehead. Then she looked across at the gang, and at his face, and understood. "Come, you and I will play," she said, and filled a bucket.

qa.q: What colour was Deepak's pichkari?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: Why did Deepak hold his stomach on the bottom stair?
qa.a: Being told he couldn't play hurt him so much that he felt it as a real tummy ache; he was sad and shocked.

qa.q: What did Dadi do well?
qa.a: She looked beyond the tummy ache, understood he had been left out, and played with him herself.

qa.q: How might Yash see his words?
qa.a: Yash probably thinks he is only keeping the game for bigger children and doesn't realise how much it hurt Deepak.

grounding: Shows a young child left out of a game freezing and complaining of a tummy ache.

passage: Before: On the first day of the Ramzan holidays' tuition week, Irfan waved to Sachin and the others by the gate. They turned away. He thought they hadn't seen. During: Three days later, in class, nobody passed him the worksheet. When he asked Sachin a question, Sachin looked straight at the board. Irfan's face went hot. What had he done? He went through everything in his head. At home he couldn't finish his food. Abbu asked what was wrong, and Irfan told him. After: The next day Abbu spoke to the tuition teacher, who sat the boys together at break. Sachin mumbled that someone said Irfan had laughed at his handwriting. "I didn't," Irfan said. It hurt that nobody had just asked.

qa.q: What did nobody pass Irfan in class?
qa.a: The worksheet.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when his friends ignored him?
qa.a: He felt anxious, confused and invisible, going over everything in his head to find what he had done wrong.

qa.q: What helped the situation, and why?
qa.a: Telling Abbu, who spoke to the tuition teacher the next day; the teacher sat the boys together so the misunderstanding could come out.

qa.q: How might Sachin see the silent treatment?
qa.a: Sachin believed a rumour that Irfan laughed at his handwriting and may have thought ignoring him was fair, not seeing how much it hurt.

grounding: Illustrates a child whose friends stop speaking to him feeling invisible, anxious and confused about what he did.

passage: Sit, Yash. You're sulking because your friends went quiet on you? Let me tell you about the Onam when I was a girl of ten. My three best friends and I made the pookalam together every year. That year, on the first morning, they just didn't call for me. At school they whispered and stopped when I came near. Nobody said a word to me. Not a single cruel word, either. That was the worst part. If they'd teased me, at least I'd know what I'd done. I stopped eating properly. Finally my amma walked me to the eldest girl's house and asked her mother to let us talk. It was over a torn ribbon I didn't even remember. Your Rukmini Ammamma cried that night, Yash, with relief.

qa.q: What did the friends make together every year?
qa.a: The pookalam.

qa.q: Why did the silence hurt Rukmini more than teasing would have?
qa.a: She felt anxious and confused because she couldn't tell what she had done; being ignored left her feeling invisible.

qa.q: What turning point in the story ended the silence?
qa.a: Her amma walked her to the eldest girl's house and asked the mother to let the girls talk, which brought out the torn ribbon misunderstanding.

qa.q: How might the eldest girl have felt when she learned it was over a forgotten ribbon?
qa.a: She might have felt embarrassed or sheepish that a small grudge caused so much hurt.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a childhood silent treatment and how being ignored hurt more than teasing.

passage: The bus to the winter picnic was full, and the fog meant it crawled. Gurpreet had saved a seat for Aman, but Aman sat with the others at the back. When Gurpreet turned around to show a drawing, they all looked out of the window together. Nobody laughed. Nobody said anything. For two hours, with no room to move and no signal on his phone, Gurpreet stared at the seat in front. He wondered what he'd done. Was it the cricket match? His stomach tightened. At the stop, Nitin from the other section sat beside him with a packet of peanuts. "Want some?" Gurpreet nodded, afraid his voice would crack. Later he told Nitin, who walked with him straight to their class teacher that afternoon.

qa.q: What did Nitin bring when he sat beside Gurpreet?
qa.a: A packet of peanuts.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet's tight stomach suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt anxious and hurt, confused about what he had done to be ignored.

qa.q: What did Nitin do that helped, and what came next?
qa.a: He sat with Gurpreet and offered peanuts, then walked with him to their class teacher that afternoon so an adult knew.

qa.q: What would change if the group had openly said what was wrong?
qa.a: Gurpreet would at least know the reason and could explain or apologise, instead of guessing for two hours.

grounding: Illustrates a child given the silent treatment on a trip, feeling invisible and anxious.

passage:
25 Dec, winter camp
Today I told everyone at the dorm not to talk to Yogesh. He showed the counsellor the pillow mess and we all got a warning. So I said, "Nobody sit with him at breakfast." And nobody did. It felt good. Like I was the one in charge, finally, and everyone listened. He deserved it. He's a snitch. But then at the bonfire, Rishi said, "Jeevan, if you tell on us, we'll do the same to you," and laughed, and I laughed too but my stomach dropped. Maybe that's why I did it. So it's him and not me. Yogesh ate alone again at dinner. He kept looking at the door. I don't feel that good now.

qa.q: What did Yogesh show the counsellor?
qa.a: The pillow mess.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan's stomach drop at the bonfire?
qa.a: Jeevan felt afraid, realising the group could turn on Jeevan just as easily, and suspects that fear is why the freeze-out happened.

qa.q: What could Jeevan do to put things right?
qa.a: Jeevan could sit with Yogesh at breakfast, tell the others to stop, and talk to the counsellor about the freeze-out.

qa.q: If you were Yogesh, what would the day feel like?
qa.a: It would feel lonely and frightening, eating alone and watching the door, for having told the truth about the mess.

passage: The Diwali holidays had brought every cousin back to the village, and the cricket ground by the pond was crowded. Imran was captain, as always. When Chetan walked up with his bat, Imran said loudly, "No teams for him. He cheated last time." He hadn't, really; he'd just argued a run-out. But the other boys laughed and turned their backs, and Imran felt tall, like the ground belonged to him. Then his older cousin arrived from the city, a better batsman, and the boys crowded around him instead. Imran's chest tightened. He glanced at Chetan sitting alone under the neem tree. Keeping Chetan out had felt like keeping himself in. Now he wasn't so sure it had worked.

qa.q: Where was the cricket ground?
qa.a: By the pond.

qa.q: Why did Imran's chest tighten when his cousin arrived?
qa.a: He felt anxious about losing his place as the boys crowded around the better batsman, the same fear that pushed him to shut Chetan out.

qa.q: What could Imran do now?
qa.a: He could invite Chetan to bat and admit to the boys that it was only an argument over a run-out, not cheating.

qa.q: What is it like for Chetan under the neem tree?
qa.a: He probably feels lonely and humiliated, excluded for an argument everyone treats as cheating.

grounding: Illustrates a child leading a group to shun a classmate, feeling powerful and acting from fear of losing his own place.

passage: In Tromsø, the polar nights made recess short and cold, and the class played snow football in the dark under floodlights. Lars always picked teams. This week he whispered to everyone, "Nobody picks Bilal." Bilal had scored against Lars's team twice. Now, each recess, Bilal stood by the fence, kicking snow, while Lars shouted names. Lars liked how quickly they obeyed. It felt safe, being the one who decides. He told himself Bilal was a show-off anyway. But on Thursday, when a new boy scored a beautiful goal and everyone cheered him instead of Lars, Lars felt a cold jolt. The teacher had noticed Bilal at the fence and called Lars aside after recess. "Tell me how teams get picked," she said.

qa.q: How many times had Bilal scored against Lars's team?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What did Lars feel when everyone cheered the new boy?
qa.a: He felt a cold jolt of fear, worried about losing his own place at the centre, which hints at why he shut Bilal out.

qa.q: How could the teacher help after asking about team-picking?
qa.a: She could make team choices fair, such as rotating captains, and talk with Lars about how Bilal feels at the fence.

qa.q: How does Bilal experience recess this week?
qa.a: He stands alone by the fence kicking snow, likely feeling rejected and confused about why nobody picks him.

grounding: Shows a child organising a group to exclude a classmate, enjoying the power and acting from fear of losing his own position.

passage: Mridul noticed it first in the canteen: Jasleen, alone at the end of the long table, eating quickly, eyes on her tiffin. Then in the class group chat, a party plan was posted, and her name wasn't in the list of people bringing things. The next week she'd left the chat altogether. Nobody mentioned it. Mridul didn't want to make a scene. So at the next biology practical, when the teacher said to form pairs, he walked over. "Want to partner? I'm terrible at slides." Jasleen looked up, surprised. "Sure." They talked about onion cells and a series both had watched. At lunch, Mridul sat two seats from her, then one. Nobody made a thing of it. By Friday two others had joined them.

qa.q: What did Jasleen do the week after the party plan was posted?
qa.a: She left the chat altogether.

qa.q: Why did Mridul choose the biology practical to approach Jasleen?
qa.a: He wanted to reach out without making a scene; he felt concerned for her but wary of drawing attention.

qa.q: What small step would help a lonely classmate, based on what Mridul did?
qa.a: Include them in an ordinary task, like pairing up, and sit near them at lunch without fuss.

qa.q: What is it like for Jasleen when Mridul asks her to partner?
qa.a: She is surprised and probably relieved, finally included in something without being singled out.

grounding: Illustrates a classmate noticing someone eating alone and dropped from chats, and breaking the cycle with a small, quiet act.

passage: "Maria's by herself again," Indu whispered to her friend. "Third day." "She left our group chat, na?" "Did she leave, or did someone remove her?" "Don't know." Indu watched Maria turn the pages of a book she clearly wasn't reading. At the next free period, Indu walked over. "Maria, we're one short for the quiz team. Want to be our science person?" "Me?" "You got full marks in that physics test." Maria hesitated. "Won't the others mind?" "It's my team," Indu said, shrugging. "Practice is after lunch. Just come." Maria nodded, a small smile. After lunch, she came. By the end, she was arguing about Newton with everyone, and nobody remembered she'd been alone.

qa.q: What did Indu ask Maria to be?
qa.a: Their science person on the quiz team.

qa.q: What does Maria's question "Won't the others mind?" suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels unsure and unwanted, worried she will be rejected again.

qa.q: How could Indu keep Maria included after the quiz?
qa.a: She could keep inviting her to practices and add her back to the group chat without making a fuss.

qa.q: How does Indu see Maria's situation?
qa.a: Indu sees that Maria has been alone for days and uses a simple task, the quiz team, to include her without drawing attention.

grounding: Shows a classmate noticing a lonely student and including her in a task quietly.

passage: I'm Chandrika, and I'm not proud that it took me three weeks to see it. Madhuri used to sit with our group at lunch. Then one day she was on the bench by the library, alone, with her tiffin on her knees. In the group chat, people started making plans in a new group I later realised she wasn't in. I kept thinking it wasn't my business. Then I saw her laugh at something on her phone, alone, and stop, like she'd remembered where she was. The next day I sat down on the library bench, not saying why. "Can I share your shade?" She moved her bag. We talked about the library's terrible fans. Now I sit there twice a week. It was such a small thing. I should have done it sooner.

qa.q: Where did Madhuri start sitting at lunch?
qa.a: On the bench by the library.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when Chandrika finally sat down?
qa.a: Chandrika felt some regret for waiting three weeks, and quiet concern for Madhuri.

qa.q: What made Chandrika's approach work?
qa.a: It was small and quiet: sitting down and asking to share the shade without drawing attention to Madhuri's loneliness.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel when someone sits on the library bench?
qa.a: Madhuri may feel relieved and less invisible, glad to be sought out without being pitied.

grounding: Illustrates a student noticing a classmate eating alone and dropped from chats, and breaking the cycle with a small act.

passage: The counselling room at the university was warm and smelled of tea. Ira kept her jacket on. "My old group made a new chat without me," she said. "I saw the photos from the trip." Her voice wobbled. "It hurts more than I expected." The counsellor waited. "Part of me wants to post my own photos and not invite them to anything." "And the other part?" "The other part knows that's what they did." Ira looked at her hands. "My lab partner, Sachin, asked me to the film club twice. I said no both times." "What if you said yes this week?" Ira nodded slowly. That Friday she went. She laughed twice. It still hurt. But she didn't think something was wrong with her.

qa.q: What did Ira see from the old group?
qa.a: The photos from the trip.

qa.q: How did Ira feel about being left out?
qa.a: She felt deeply hurt, and also tempted to get back at them by excluding them in return.

qa.q: What helped Ira most, and why?
qa.a: Saying yes to Sachin's invitation to the film club, because it connected her with people who wanted her there.

qa.q: What might Sachin think when Ira finally comes to the film club?
qa.a: He might feel pleased that she finally accepted, not knowing how hard the week had been for her.

grounding: Shows a young adult excluded from a friend circle admitting the hurt, reaching out to others and not retaliating.

passage:
Dear Simran,
It's been ages. I'm writing because you once told me honesty works better than pretending. So here it is. The friends I made in first year have drifted into a new circle, and I'm not in it. I found out when I saw a birthday dinner I didn't know about. I sulked for a week. I drafted a sarcastic message and deleted it. I thought about not inviting any of them to my birthday. I won't. That's their way, not mine. I've started having tea with two people from my department instead, and last Sunday I called Mummy and admitted it hurt. I'm okay. I'm not broken. I just miss being known, so I'm writing to someone who knows me.
Nitin

qa.q: How did Nitin find out about the new circle?
qa.a: By seeing a birthday dinner Nitin didn't know about.

qa.q: What does "I'm not broken" suggest about how Nitin feels?
qa.a: It suggests Nitin still feels hurt and lonely but has decided the exclusion does not mean something is wrong with Nitin.

qa.q: Which choices in the letter helped Nitin cope?
qa.a: Admitting the hurt to Mummy, deleting the sarcastic message, not retaliating, and reaching out to new people and to Simran.

qa.q: How might Simran feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Simran might feel touched and trusted, glad to be the one Nitin turned to.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult shut out of a circle who admits the hurt, reaches out elsewhere and refuses to retaliate.

passage: Rashmi, you asked why I stopped mentioning the flat girls. Honestly? They planned the whole Goa trip in a chat without me. I only found out from the tickets on the table. I cried in the bathroom. Then I got angry. I wanted to plan something with the others in class and pointedly not ask them. I even started the chat. Then I deleted it. It would have been me doing the same thing. So I did the boring stuff instead. I told one of them, calmly, that it hurt. She said sorry, sort of. I started going to the running group on Sundays. I call you more, as you've noticed. I'm fine. Some days are hard. That's all it is. I'm Ritu, not some leftover.

qa.q: How did Ritu find out about the Goa trip?
qa.a: From the tickets on the table.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling after finding out?
qa.a: Ritu felt deeply hurt, crying in the bathroom, then angry enough to want revenge by excluding them.

qa.q: What choice did Ritu make instead of retaliating, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Ritu deleted the revenge chat, calmly told one flatmate it hurt, and joined the running group, keeping self-respect without hurting others.

qa.q: How might Rashmi see Ritu's recent calls?
qa.a: Rashmi noticed Ritu calling more and may feel glad to be trusted and supportive in a hard time.

grounding: Shows a young adult shut out by flatmates admitting the hurt, reaching out and avoiding revenge exclusion.
